**New airport clinic aims to treat travelers’ minor illnesses before they take off**

*By [Reporter Name]*

ATLANTA — For travelers rushing through the world’s busiest airport, a sore throat, earache or sudden fever can quickly turn a long-awaited trip into a logistical headache. Now, a new medical clinic at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is offering passengers another option: walk-in care without leaving the terminal.

The clinic, located inside the airport, is designed to treat minor illnesses and travel-related health concerns — from colds, sinus infections and nausea to minor cuts, sprains, rashes and medication questions. Airport officials say the goal is to help travelers get timely care while reducing unnecessary emergency room visits and avoiding disruptions to travel plans when it’s medically appropriate.

For Atlanta traveler **Maria Thompson**, the clinic came as a relief after she developed a painful earache before a flight to Denver.

“I was worried I’d have to cancel or find an urgent care outside the airport,” Thompson said. “Being able to see someone right there before boarding made a huge difference.”

Clinicians evaluated her symptoms, discussed whether flying could worsen her discomfort and recommended treatment options. Thompson said she was able to continue her trip with a clearer understanding of what to watch for.

Health experts say airport clinics can fill an important gap, especially for passengers who may be far from their regular doctors.

“Travelers often ignore symptoms because they don’t want to miss a flight, but some minor conditions can become more serious if they’re not addressed,” said **Dr. Elaine Porter**, an emergency medicine physician familiar with travel health services. “Having access to basic medical evaluation in the airport can help people make safer decisions.”

The clinic is not intended to replace emergency care. Patients with chest pain, difficulty breathing, stroke symptoms, severe allergic reactions, major injuries or other urgent warning signs should call 911 or seek emergency medical attention immediately, clinicians say.

But for less severe concerns, airport-based care can be particularly useful. Common travel issues include dehydration, motion sickness, gastrointestinal symptoms, respiratory infections, anxiety, ear pain from congestion and minor injuries from luggage or falls.

Another passenger, **James Whitfield**, said he stopped by after developing a rash during a layover on his way home from a business trip.

“I didn’t know if it was something I picked up from a hotel or maybe an allergic reaction,” Whitfield said. “I just wanted someone to look at it before I got on another plane.”

According to travel medicine specialists, convenience is only part of the equation. Airport clinics may also help identify when passengers should delay travel.

“Flying while ill isn’t always just uncomfortable — in some cases it can be risky for the traveler or for others nearby,” said **Dr. Karen Liu**, a travel medicine expert. “A medical professional can help assess whether symptoms are mild or whether they suggest something that needs more urgent follow-up.”

Airport officials say the clinic also supports employees, including airline staff, concession workers and other airport personnel who may need quick access to care during long shifts.

Public health experts note that the pandemic changed how many travelers think about symptoms such as cough, fever and fatigue. While most airports have moved away from large-scale health screening, they say easy access to medical advice remains valuable.

“People are more aware now that respiratory symptoms matter,” Porter said. “If you’re sick before a flight, it’s reasonable to ask: Do I need testing? Should I mask? Should I postpone travel? A clinic can help answer those questions.”

For passengers, the advice remains straightforward: plan ahead, carry essential medications, stay hydrated and don’t ignore worsening symptoms.

As for Thompson, she said the clinic helped salvage her trip.

“When you’re traveling, everything feels urgent,” she said. “It was nice to have medical care in the middle of all that chaos.”

**Medical News Feature**  
**Atlanta — Retail Health Clinics Take Off at Airports**

ATLANTA — For travelers who develop a fever between flights, forget a prescription at home, or need a quick check for an ear infection before boarding, the airport is increasingly becoming more than a place to catch a plane. It is becoming a place to see a clinician.

At Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, one of the world’s busiest passenger hubs, **The AeroClinic** is part of a growing trend: retail-style health clinics moving into airports to serve travelers, airline employees, airport workers and nearby residents who need convenient, basic medical care without a trip to an emergency room.

The clinic operates much like the walk-in clinics that have expanded through drugstores and shopping centers across the country. Patients can be seen for common, low-acuity medical problems, often without an appointment, and typically at a lower cost than hospital-based urgent or emergency care.

### Care for Travelers in a Hurry

The AeroClinic’s menu of services is aimed at the realities of travel. Clinicians can evaluate and treat common illnesses such as colds, flu-like symptoms, sinus infections, sore throats, ear pain, minor skin problems, allergies, urinary symptoms and stomach complaints. The clinic also may provide basic travel-related care, including vaccinations, medication refills when appropriate, and treatment for minor injuries such as sprains, cuts or rashes.

For airport and airline employees, the clinic can function as a convenient workplace health option. For passengers, it offers another choice when symptoms arise suddenly before a flight or during a layover.

The concept is simple: instead of leaving the airport campus, calling off a trip, or turning to an emergency department for a non-emergency condition, patients can receive basic evaluation and treatment on site.

### Costs Lower Than the Emergency Room

One of the clinic’s main selling points is price transparency. Retail clinics generally charge far less than emergency departments for routine problems, and The AeroClinic follows that model with posted charges for common visits and services.

The cost of a visit depends on the type of care provided, but routine evaluations are typically priced in the range of a standard retail clinic or urgent-care visit rather than an emergency room bill. Additional services — such as laboratory testing, vaccines, medications or procedures — may cost extra.

For travelers without a regular physician nearby, that can be an important distinction. A sore throat or ear infection treated in an emergency department can result in a bill many times higher than a walk-in clinic visit. The AeroClinic is designed for conditions that do not require hospital-level care.

### Not a Substitute for Emergency Care

Clinic leaders stress that the airport location does not make The AeroClinic an emergency department. Its clinicians are not equipped to manage life-threatening problems such as chest pain, stroke symptoms, severe allergic reactions, major trauma, uncontrolled bleeding, severe shortness of breath or complicated medical emergencies.

Patients with serious symptoms are directed to emergency medical services or a hospital.

The clinic also has limits on what it will prescribe. Like many retail clinics, it is not intended as a source for narcotic pain medicines or controlled substances, and it does not replace ongoing primary care for chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart disease, severe asthma or complex psychiatric illness.

Instead, the model is built around convenience care: quick access for limited, common problems.

### Airports as the Next Retail Health Frontier

Retail clinics have become a familiar part of the health-care landscape over the past two decades, driven by consumer demand for walk-in access, evening and weekend hours, and upfront pricing. Airports are a natural extension of that strategy.

Major airports contain the population of a small city on any given day. Hartsfield-Jackson moves huge volumes of passengers while also serving thousands of airline, concession, security, maintenance and airport employees. That creates a built-in patient base, many of whom may not have easy access to their regular doctor while at work or in transit.

The airport setting also fills a gap for travelers who are too sick to fly comfortably but not sick enough for the ER — or those who need documentation, advice or medication before continuing a trip.

### Expansion Planned for Philadelphia

The AeroClinic is not stopping in Atlanta. The company has announced plans to open a clinic at **Philadelphia International Airport**, bringing the same airport-based retail health model to another major travel hub.

The Philadelphia location is expected to offer similar services: walk-in treatment for minor illnesses and injuries, basic testing, travel-related care and occupational health support for airport workers. If successful, the model could spread to additional airports where passenger traffic and employee demand make on-site medical services practical.

### A Changing Definition of Access

The rise of airport clinics reflects a broader shift in health care: patients increasingly expect medical services to be available where they already are — at pharmacies, workplaces, shopping centers and now airline terminals.

For physicians and health policy experts, the trend raises familiar questions about continuity of care, appropriate prescribing and coordination with a patient’s regular doctor. But for a traveler facing a painful ear infection before a transatlantic flight, convenience can be decisive.

The AeroClinic’s niche is not comprehensive medicine. It is timely, limited care in a place where time is often the traveler’s scarcest resource.

As airports continue to evolve into full-service commercial centers, medical clinics may become as routine as coffee shops and charging stations — another stop before takeoff.

For passengers facing an unexpected illness at the airport, though, the clinic may offer a welcome alternative: medical help just steps from the gate, without a detour to the hospital.

# Airport Clinics Offer a Faster Alternative to the ER for Travelers and Airport Workers

For frequent fliers and airport employees, illness and injury often happen at the worst possible time: between flights, during a shift, or far from a regular doctor. In those moments, the default choice has often been the emergency room — even for problems that are urgent but not life-threatening.

Airport clinics are increasingly filling that gap. Located inside or near major terminals, these medical offices provide walk-in care for passengers, flight crews, airline staff, concessions workers, TSA employees, and others who spend much of their time in and around airports. They can treat common travel-related illnesses, minor injuries, infections, dehydration, work-related strains, and other conditions that do not require a full hospital emergency department.

The experiences of frequent traveler Stephen Plumlee and airport worker Derrick Gross show why these clinics can be a practical alternative.

## A Convenient Option for Frequent Fliers

Stephen Plumlee represents the kind of patient airport clinics are designed to help: someone who travels often and cannot easily pause his schedule for a traditional doctor’s visit.

For frequent fliers, medical issues can become complicated quickly. A sinus infection may worsen during a long flight. A stomach illness can make travel impossible. A minor injury can become difficult to manage while moving through terminals, rental car lots, and hotels. Yet going to an emergency room can mean hours of waiting, high costs, and missed flights.

An airport clinic offers a middle path. Instead of leaving the airport campus, finding a hospital, and potentially losing an entire day, a traveler like Plumlee can seek care close to the gate or terminal. Clinicians can evaluate symptoms, provide basic treatment, prescribe medication when appropriate, and advise whether it is safe to fly.

For many travelers, that is the key advantage: airport clinics understand the time pressure of air travel. Their patients are often trying to determine whether they can board a flight, continue a business trip, or need more serious medical attention. The clinic can help make that decision quickly and safely.

## Care for the Airport Workforce

Derrick Gross illustrates another major group served by airport clinics: the people who work at the airport every day.

Airports operate like small cities. Thousands of employees handle baggage, clean aircraft, prepare food, provide security, assist passengers, maintain facilities, fuel planes, and manage ground transportation. Many work long shifts, perform physically demanding tasks, and may not have easy access to a primary-care provider during normal office hours.

For workers like Gross, an airport clinic can be especially valuable because it is close to the job site. Instead of leaving work for an off-site urgent care center or spending hours in an emergency room, employees can get treatment for minor injuries or illnesses nearby.

That can matter for both health and employment. A worker with a strained back, cut, respiratory infection, or eye irritation may need prompt evaluation. The clinic can provide first-line treatment, document the visit, recommend work restrictions if necessary, and help determine whether the employee needs follow-up care.

For employers, having a clinic nearby can also reduce lost work time and help employees address medical concerns before they become more serious.

## What Airport Clinics Commonly Treat

Airport clinics are not meant to replace hospitals. But they are well suited for non-emergency conditions that still require timely care. Common services may include:

- Treatment for colds, flu, sore throats, ear pain, and sinus infections  
- Care for nausea, dehydration, food-related illness, and minor stomach problems  
- Evaluation of sprains, strains, minor cuts, and bruises  
- Basic wound care and bandaging  
- Blood pressure checks and other routine assessments  
- Prescription refills or short-term medication needs, when appropriate  
- Travel medicine advice, depending on the clinic  
- Occupational health services for airport workers  
- Referrals to emergency departments when a condition is serious  

For a passenger with chest pain, signs of stroke, severe allergic reaction, major trauma, or difficulty breathing, the emergency room — or emergency medical services — remains the right choice. Airport clinics are most useful for cases that are urgent but not life-threatening.

## Why Patients Choose the Clinic Over the ER

The appeal comes down to four main factors: speed, location, cost, and familiarity with airport life.

Emergency rooms must prioritize the sickest patients first, which means someone with a minor condition may wait a long time. Airport clinics, by contrast, typically function more like urgent care centers. They can often see walk-in patients more quickly for routine problems.

Location is another major advantage. For travelers, leaving the airport can mean missing a flight or disrupting an itinerary. For employees, it can mean lost wages or schedule complications. A clinic inside the airport reduces those barriers.

Cost is also a factor. Emergency room visits are often expensive, especially for minor conditions that could be treated in a lower-acuity setting. While prices and insurance coverage vary, clinic-based care is often less costly than an ER visit.

Finally, airport clinics understand the unique needs of their patient population. They know travelers may need documentation for airlines, guidance on whether flying is safe, or help managing symptoms during a trip. They also understand the physical demands placed on airport workers.

## Case Studies: Plumlee and Gross

Stephen Plumlee’s case shows the value of access for travelers. When someone is frequently on the road, even a minor illness can interfere with work, family obligations, and travel plans. An airport clinic can provide quick evaluation and treatment without forcing a major detour to a hospital.

Derrick Gross’s case highlights the workplace side of the same issue. Airport employees need health care that fits the reality of shift work and a fast-moving environment. For them, an on-site clinic can mean getting help early, returning to work safely, or being directed to more advanced care when needed.

Together, their experiences demonstrate how airport clinics serve two overlapping communities: people passing through and people who keep the airport running.

## A Complement, Not a Replacement

Airport clinics are not a substitute for emergency departments. Serious or life-threatening symptoms require immediate emergency care. But many airport medical problems fall into a gray area: too uncomfortable or concerning to ignore, but not severe enough to justify a hospital ER.

For those situations, airport clinics can provide an important alternative. They reduce unnecessary emergency room visits, give travelers and workers faster access to care, and help keep the airport moving.

For frequent fliers like Stephen Plumlee and airport employees like Derrick Gross, that can make the difference between a medical problem that derails the day and one that is handled quickly, safely, and close to where they already are.
